Konysz-Taperek (Succession de)

2016 QCCS 5101

SUPERIOR COURT

(
Civil Division
)

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

No:

500-17-066352-116

DATE:

October 12, 2016

_____________________________________________________________________

PRESIDED
BY

THE HONOURABLE

STEPHEN W.
HAMILTON, J.S.C.

_____________________________________________________________________

TERESA TAPEREK

Plaintiff

v.

RICHARD TAPEREK, personally
and ès qualité

liquidator to the SUCCESSION
OF THE LATE

EMILIA KONYSZ-TAPEREK

And

JADWIGA TAPEREK CIOCHON,
personally and ès qualité

liquidator to the SUCCESSION
OF THE LATE

EMILIA KONYSZ-TAPEREK

Defendants

And

HALINA TAPEREK

FRANK TAPEREK

DONNA TAPEREK

THE REGISTRAR FOR THE LAND

REGISTRY FOR THE DIVISION OF
MONTREAL

Mis en cause

_____________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

_____________________________________________________________________

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

The mother signed a number of wills and codicils
in the 19 months before she passed away, whereby she reduced the inheritance of
her eldest daughter and ultimately disinherited her completely.

[
2
]

The eldest daughter now asks the Court to annul
those wills and codicils on the basis that the mother was unduly influenced by
her other children or did not have the required testamentary capacity.

[
3
]

The other children contest the action and seek
to uphold the wills and codicils.

Context

[
4
]

The parties are all members of the same family.

[
5
]

The father, Rudolf Taperek, had fought with the
Polish Army in the Second World War. He came to Canada after the war and worked
until he suffered a work accident in the late 1970s. The mother Emilia Konyz
was also born in Poland and came to Canada after the war. She did not work
outside the house.

[
6
]

They married in 1950 and had six children:
Teresa (born 1951), Halina (born 1952), Jadwiga (born 1955), Richard (born
1957), Frank (born 1969) and Donna (born 1972).
[1]

[
7
]

They acquired four properties during their
lifetimes: a duplex at 3502-3504 Cuvillier Street, a duplex at 2525-2527 Bercy
Street (which they built in 1972) and a house at 2648 Wurtele Street, all in
Montreal, as well as some vacant land in St-Hubert.

[
8
]

In 2000, the parents were living in the lower
duplex on Bercy. The father was 86 years old and was living off his work
pension and his veteran’s pension. The mother was 71. Both had a variety of
health issues. Teresa had been living in the duplex on Cuvillier since 1981.

[
9
]

The parents both had wills dated August 13,
1989.
[2]
The 1989 wills divided the properties among the children. Teresa
was to receive Cuvillier, half of the land in St-Hubert and one-sixth of the
remaining property after the death of the surviving spouse. She was the sole
liquidator.

[
10
]

On July 1, 2000, Donna moved to Cuvillier. She
had been diagnosed with multiple sclerosis and the father wanted her closer.
Teresa moved into the upper duplex on Bercy.

[
11
]

All of the parties agree that Teresa became the
principal caregiver for the parents. Teresa says that she did not get much help
from her siblings, but they do not agree with that assessment. Teresa also
testified that she gave up her career to care for the parents. The siblings
contest this.

[
12
]

On August 18, 2005, the parents executed new
wills before Notary Andrea F. Durso.
[3]
The
2005 wills provide that each spouse left everything to the other and that the
surviving spouse left everything to the six children equally, with Jadwiga and
Richard as liquidators.

[
13
]

The siblings testified that Teresa was angry
over the new wills, which led to a falling out between Teresa and the parents.
Teresa testified that the falling out was unrelated to the new wills, which
were executed after the falling out. The parties also disagree on the duration
of the falling out. Teresa said it was two months and the siblings testified
that it was over a year.

[
14
]

In any event, the siblings stepped in to look
after the parents during the falling out, and Teresa resumed her role as
principal caregiver for the parents in 2005 or 2006. All of the doctors who
testified confirmed that Teresa brought the parents to all of their medical
appointments over the years, with very few exceptions. Donna kept
responsibility for the mother’s finances.

[
15
]

On January 23, 2008, Teresa brought the parents
to Notary Durso to execute codicils to their 2005 wills.
[4]

Pursuant to the 2008 codicils, on the death of the surviving spouse, Donna was
to receive Cuvillier and Teresa was to receive one-half of Bercy, with the
residue of the estate to be divided amongst the five children other than Donna.
Teresa and Richard were the liquidators. The 2008 codicils were not disclosed
to the siblings.

[
16
]

The father passed away on March 4, 2009, at the
age of 95.
[5]

[
17
]

Richard and Jadwiga, assuming that the 2005 will
was still in force and that they were the liquidators of the father’s estate,
started sorting some of his belongings such as his clothing and had the mail
redirected to Richard’s address so that he could deal with it.

[
18
]

A few days later, the mother told them that
Jadwiga was no longer a liquidator of the father’s estate. According to Richard
and Jadwiga, the mother also said that Teresa had taken them to the notary to
change their wills and that she wanted to change her will back to what it was
before.

[
19
]

Richard and Jadwiga brought the mother to see
Notary Durso and she executed a new will
[6]
and
mandate
[7]
on March 16, 2009. The new will provided for an equal division of
her estate among the six children. Richard and Jadwiga were the liquidators
under the will and the mandataries under the mandate, with Donna as
replacement. This had the effect of cancelling the January 2008 codicil and
going back to the August 2005 will.

[
20
]

Richard and Jadwiga told the other siblings
about the new will. Richard testified that Donna agreed that it was not fair
that she receive more than the others. This new will was not disclosed to
Teresa.

[
21
]

Madeleine Fortin, the social worker with the
CLSC responsible for the parents, met with the mother, as well as Teresa,
Richard and Jadwiga, on March 10, 2009 to see how the mother was doing and to
assess whether she was able to stay in Bercy and whether she needed more
services from the CLSC. Fortin concluded that the mother needed constant care
and she suggested that Teresa move downstairs. Teresa said that she had a baby
monitor and did not need to move downstairs. Fortin also suggested that the
mother should be moved to a nursing home. She explained that the first step
would be to put the mother’s name on a waiting list, and that the wait would
likely be as long as 2½ years. The mother indicated that she did not want to go
to a nursing home. Teresa supported the mother’s position. Richard and Jadwiga
wanted the mother to at least put her name on the waiting list. Teresa was
upset and went upstairs. There was supposed to be a follow up meeting with
Fortin to complete the form to put her name on the waiting list.

[
22
]

Meanwhile Richard and Teresa, as liquidators of
the father’s estate, took some preliminary steps in March.
[8]
Teresa alleges that Richard removed the title deeds to the
properties from the parents’ duplex, and that Richard and the others removed a
number of the father’s personal effects. Richard said that he was trying to
organize the father’s affairs and that Teresa was not helping.

[
23
]

On April 8, 2009, Teresa, concerned about what
her siblings were doing, took the mother to see Notary Raphael H. Salama to
execute a new mandate in her favour.
[9]

Teresa did not advise her siblings of the new mandate.
[10]

[
24
]

In that same time period, the siblings became
concerned about the mother. She went to Jadwiga’s for Easter dinner on April
12, but she was not herself and did not say much. The next day, they could not
reach her by telephone and they discovered that Teresa had changed the locks on
the mother’s duplex. There was a confrontation between Teresa and Donna. When
Richard and Jadwiga came later that evening, Teresa would not open the door.
They called the police. Teresa finally opened the door when the police came and
the police found the mother sitting in the dark.
[11]
The
police were called on two more occasions that week, on April 17 by a niece to
ask the police to check on the mother
[12]
and
on April 18 by Teresa because the mother had let Jadwiga in. On each occasion,
the police noted that the mother was well and she said that she was alright and
did not want to leave. Richard spoke to the mother by telephone only once that
week. He testified that the mother told him that Teresa unplugged the telephone
because the mother talked too much but that the mother had plugged the
telephone back in when Teresa went out. The police told Teresa that she is not
allowed to unplug the telephone. Teresa subsequently began the process to
change the mother’s telephone number. Teresa said that the siblings were
harassing the mother about moving to a nursing home and were taking things.

[
25
]

Jadwiga called Fortin to tell her that they did
not have access to the mother and that Teresa had unplugged the phones and
changed the locks.

[
26
]

Fortin was aware of the mother’s health issues
and the siblings had told her about some issues relating to wills and mandates
and Teresa’s administration of the parents’ affairs.

[
27
]

There were also scheduled visits from the CLSC
to assist the mother with baths and house cleaning and to give Teresa respite.
According to Fortin, Teresa cancelled these visits in April. Teresa denies this.
[13]

[
28
]

Fortin decided to visit the mother to ensure
that everything was alright. She made several calls to the mother and to Teresa
but no one answered. She left a message for Teresa that she was coming to visit
the mother.
[14]
She went to the house two or three times. No one answered the door.
Teresa says that she was not aware of any such visit and that she took the
mother out for the day. They even went to see a movie and did not arrive home
until 10 pm.

[
29
]

When Fortin was unable to visit the mother, she
became very concerned as to the mother’s well-being. Fortin made a motion to
the Cour du Québec on April 23 asking for a psychiatric evaluation of the
mother.
[15]
The motion was granted the same day.
[16]

Fortin advised Jadwiga that she was doing this but told Jadwiga that she could
not be there when the order was executed.

[
30
]

When the police attempted to execute the order
on April 24 at 9:15 am, Teresa did not answer the door. She testified that she
heard someone at the door but it looked like Jadwiga, her son Adam and maybe
his girlfriend so she decided to ignore it. The police officer testified that
two of the people were wearing police uniforms and they identified themselves
verbally when they knocked on the front door, the back door and the windows.
After 90 minutes, the police opened the door with the assistance of a locksmith
and took the mother to Hôpital Notre-Dame for a psychiatric evaluation.
[17]

[
31
]

The siblings went to the hospital everyday that
week. They testified that the mother seemed more herself while she was at the
hospital. She seemed relieved and comfortable, and to be happy to be out of her
house.

[
32
]

The mother said that she did not want to see
Teresa and the hospital staff did not allow Teresa to see her. Teresa went to
the hospital on April 28. The head nurse spoke to the mother and told Teresa
that the mother did not want to see her, and security guards escorted Teresa
out of the building.

[
33
]

The mother passed the psychiatric evaluation.
[18]

[
34
]

There was a meeting on April 30 at the hospital
for the family to meet with the various professionals involved in the mother’s
case.

[
35
]

The professionals concluded that the mother
could not return home because of her limited mobility and the risk of a fall,
and that she should be placed in a nursing home. The mother accepted that conclusion.
Only Teresa dissented. She insisted that she could look after the mother on
Bercy.
[19]

[
36
]

At the end of the meeting, Jadwiga asked for
permission to take the mother out of the hospital on May 2 for the mother’s 80
th

birthday. The professionals agreed. Teresa asked for permission to take her out
the next day, but this was refused. The mother did not want to go with Teresa.

[
37
]

During the meeting, Fortin asked Teresa to give
Richard a key to the mother’s house, which she did. Fortin reminded the mother
that there was something that she wanted to say. The mother said that she had
signed something at the notary and was not sure exactly what, but she wanted to
go to the notary as soon as possible to fix it.

[
38
]

Richard brought the mother to see Notary Durso.
The mother executed a new will
[20]
and mandate
[21]
on May 4. The terms were identical to those of the documents
executed on March 12.

[
39
]

On May 2, Richard took the mother home to pick
up some things in preparation for her 80
th
birthday party at
Jadwiga’s. When she arrived home, she found that many of her things, including
pictures, dishes, glasses, clothes and furniture were missing. The mother was
very upset. When Teresa came downstairs, the mother confronted her and demanded
to know where her things were. According to Richard, the mother told Teresa
that she needed help and told her not to come to her party. Teresa testified at
trial that after she was forced to give Richard the new key on April 30, she
was concerned that he would take things so she packed some things up and hid
them in the duplex.

[
40
]

Ultimately, Jadwiga called the police to
complain that Teresa had taken things. The police came to see Teresa with a
list of the things that had supposedly been taken but found that most of the
things were there. The police told her to return everything within a couple of
days. Teresa testified that she put everything back.
[22]

[
41
]

On May 3, the day after the birthday party,
Teresa went to the hospital to take the mother out. The mother said that she
was not going out and Teresa insisted. The nurse told Teresa to leave.

[
42
]

Teresa testified that she next spoke to the
mother on May 9. The mother told her that she had been to see Notary Durso on
May 4, and she told Teresa that Teresa was crazy and not right in the head and
needed to see a doctor.

[
43
]

Meanwhile, the mother was transferred to Jewish
Elder Care on May 11, 2009 while Richard and Jadwiga found a suitable home for
her.
[23]
Richard testified that the family other than Teresa visited her
often while she was at Jewish Elder Care and that she was happy there. The
mother went to Jadwiga’s on weekends. The mother had a telephone in her room.
She telephoned Teresa to say that she needed some things that were at the
duplex but that she did not want to see Teresa and so Richard or Donna would come
and get them. Teresa brought the things on May 28 but ended up leaving them
with a security guard because the mother was out. The mother called Teresa
again after a security guard complained to her that Teresa has accused him of
taking things. The siblings testified as to a few other telephone calls from
Teresa which seemed to upset the mother. The mother told Teresa on several
occasions that she did not want to talk to her. Teresa visited the mother at
least once and took her out to the garden. Donna found them and took the mother
back to her room. Donna testified that the mother said that she did not want to
go with Teresa but could not say no in front of strangers. Teresa testified
that the mother was very pleased to see her.

[
44
]

The mother was transferred to the Centre
d’hébergement Nazaire-Piché in Lachine on July 4, 2009.
[24]
The
family (other than Teresa) visited her often and took her out. The mother went
to Jadwiga’s house on weekends and went to Bercy. The mother participated in
activities at Nazaire-Piché. Richard described her as happy and alert.

[
45
]

The mother told the staff at Nazaire-Piché that
she did not want Teresa to visit her.
[25]

Jadwiga also told the nurse that the mother did not want Teresa to visit and
gave them a picture of Teresa.
[26]
The mother had a telephone in her room but she never called Teresa.
When Teresa asked Richard where the mother was living, he told her to ask the
mother. The mother did not tell her and told the family not to tell Teresa
where she was living because she did not want Teresa to visit her.

[
46
]

Teresa saw the mother on a few occasions when
she visited Bercy during the renovations. The siblings testified that Teresa
tried to speak to the mother on these occasions, but the mother did not want to
speak to Teresa. Teresa testified that the mother was always happy to see her.

[
47
]

Meanwhile, the problems continued. Starting in
June 2009, Teresa refused to produce certain documents relevant to the father’s
estate that Richard was asking for. The mother was upset about this. The mother
decided to sell Bercy, but there were renovations that needed to be done before
it could be sold. Richard began the renovation work in the summer of 2009. In
July, the mother sent a letter to Teresa demanding that she pay rent for the
upper duplex on Bercy and that she give Richard access in order to make
renovations.
[27]
In August, Teresa demanded information from Richard as to the
administration of the father’s estate, as well as the name of the residence
where the mother was living and a copy of the power of attorney signed in May
or June 2009.
[28]

[
48
]

The dispute relating to the father’s estate
resulted in proceedings filed by Richard against Teresa in Court record
500-14-034233-098 on August 28, 2009
[29]
and
by Teresa against Richard in Court record 500-14-034255-091 on September 2,
2009.
[30]
While these disputes were ongoing, the
mother executed a codicil to her will before Notary Durso on September 14,
2009.
[31]
The codicil provides that, in view of the problems caused by Teresa
in relation to the father’s estate, any legal fees and disbursements are to be
deducted from Teresa’s share of the mother’s estate and shared among the other
five siblings.

[
49
]

The proceedings relating to the father’s estate were
settled out of court on November 10, 2009.
[32]
Teresa delivered the keys, the title deeds and some tax returns. The
mother saw Teresa at the courthouse that day, but refused to speak to her and
refused to read the letter that Teresa’s lawyer gave her from Teresa. She said
it was too late.

[
50
]

The dispute with respect to the rent for the upper
duplex led to a further mise en demeure sent by the mother on December 7, 2009,
[33]
and proceedings before the Régie du logement by Richard on behalf
of the mother against Teresa on December 11, 2009.
[34]

[
51
]

On December 28, 2009, the mother sent a letter
to Notary Durso telling him that she wished to modify her will to disinherit
Teresa.
[35]
The letter alleges a number of complaints about Teresa, including:

•

Keeping the mother as a prisoner in her own
house and putting ideas in her head about the rest of the family in April;

•

Removing the mother’s things from Bercy in May;

•

Refusing to get a job;

•

Not paying any rent and having the parents pay
her expenses and her credit card bills;

•

Taking the proceeds from the mother’s brother’s
estate;

•

Taking money from the mother’s bank account and
putting the mother’s investments in Teresa’s name;

•

Forcing the mother to hire a lawyer; and

•

Pushing the family away.

[
52
]

Notary Durso declined to execute a new will or a
codicil and Richard brought the mother to see Notary Agnieszka Swierzbinska on
January 13, 2010 with the same instructions, this time in Polish.
[36]
Notary Swierzbinska asked Richard to obtain evidence of the
mother’s testamentary capacity.

[
53
]

There was a hearing at the Régie du logement on
January 21, 2010 at which the mother, Teresa, Richard, Jadwiga and possibly
Donna were all present. Teresa produced an annex to the lease signed by the
father in 2008 which provided that rent had been paid in advance for three
years.
[37]
No other family member was aware of this document. The mother was
very upset and accused Teresa of lying. The proceedings were discontinued on
January 28, 2010.
[38]

[
54
]

After Richard obtained evidence of the mother’s
testamentary capacity, Notary Swierzbinska prepared a new will
[39]
and mandate,
[40]
which the mother executed on March 26, 2010. Under the new will,
the mother disinherited Teresa and left her estate to her other five children
equally. Jadwiga and Richard were the liquidators under the will and the
mandataries under the mandate.

[
55
]

There were further issues and further proceedings
before the Régie du logement in June 2010 when Teresa denied access to the
upper duplex for the purpose of carrying out repairs and having potential
purchasers visit the premises. On October 8, 2010, the Régie du logement
ordered Teresa to give access.

[
56
]

The mother passed away on October 16, 2010.
[41]
Teresa was told that the mother was dying and she came to see her
on October 14, 2010.

[
57
]

The mother’s estate is worth approximately
$500,000.
[42]

[
58
]

The litigation with respect to access to the
upper duplex continued after the mother’s death, including proceedings in
injunction by Richard and Jadwiga against Teresa which were served on June 28,
2011.
[43]

[
59
]

The present proceedings were instituted by
Teresa the same day.

POSITION OF THE
PARTIES

[
60
]

Teresa argues that when the mother signed the
last four wills or codicils, she was (1) under undue influence,
[44]
or (2) subsidiarily, not mentally apt. As a result, Teresa asks the
Court to annul the wills or codicils dated March 16, 2009; May 4, 2009;
September 14, 2009; and March 26, 2010.

[
61
]

Teresa recognizes that she does not have direct
proof of undue influence, but says that is because she was not allowed to see
the mother in the last 18 months of her life. She argues that the Court should
use logic and common sense to presume undue influence based on the sequence of
events.

[
62
]

There are a number of other conclusions that
flow from the nullity of the wills and codicils, including a declaration that
Teresa owns a one-half interest in Bercy with the right to occupy the upper
duplex, the replacement of Richard and Jadwiga as liquidators, and orders to
provide an inventory and an accounting of the estate and to return any assets
removed. Teresa also asks for $100,000 punitive damages and judicial costs.

[
63
]

Finally, Teresa also argues that Richard owes
money to her or to the father’s estate for various loans made directly by her,
by her through the father or directly by the father
[45]
,
which have not been repaid.
[46]
There is no specific conclusion related to
these loans and the Court will not deal with this issue in this judgment.

[
64
]

The siblings argue that the Court should uphold
the wills and codicils made by the mother. They argue that the mother had
physical problems but that she had testamentary capacity throughout this
period, and that the wills and codicils reflect her free will. They ask the
Court to look at the wills and codicils in the context in which they were
executed, and not to infer undue influence simply because Teresa is not happy
with the choices the mother made.

Issues

[
65
]

The Court must assess whether the mother was
unduly influenced by the siblings at the time that she executed the last four
wills or codicils and whether she had capacity to execute those wills and
codicils.

[
66
]

It is important to stress that the Court is not
called upon to evaluate whether the mother’s decision to disinherit Teresa was
fair, right or appropriate. The Court cannot set aside a will or a codicil
simply because it may disagree with what the mother has done.

[
67
]

The contents of the wills and codicils are,
however, relevant. Teresa argues that the contents of the wills and codicils
show that the mother was unduly influenced by the siblings and that she lacked
capacity.

[
68
]

As preliminary matters, the Court will dispose
of a number of issues:

1.

The legal test to be applied in assessing the
mother’s capacity to execute a will or a codicil;

2.

The legal test to be applied in assessing
whether the mother was unduly influenced by the siblings;

3.

The nature of the evidence presented; and

4.

The hearsay objections that were made with
respect to witnesses repeating things that they had been told by others,
particularly the mother.

[
69
]

The Court will then consider each of the wills
or codicils in chronological order, and will examine the circumstances
surrounding the execution of each one.

[
70
]

Finally, the Court will consider the evidence as
to the mother’s capacity and any undue influence at the time of execution of
each will or codicil.

Analysis

1.

Legal test for capacity

[
71
]

Article 703
of the
Civil Code of Quebec

(C.C.Q.) provides that the testator must have “the required capacity” in order
to make a valid will:

703.

Every person
having the required capacity may, by will, provide
otherwise than as
by law for the devolution upon his death of the whole or part of his property.

[
72
]

The notion of capacity is not further defined in
the title on wills. Articles 707 to 711 C.C.Q. make up the chapter entitled
“The Capacity Required to Make a Will”. Article 707 C.C.Q. adds that the
testator’s capacity is assessed at the time that he or she made the will:

707.

The capacity of
the testator is considered relatively to the time he made his will.

[
73
]

The remaining articles in the chapter deal with
minors, persons of full age under tutorship or curatorship, and tutors,
curators and advisers.

[
74
]

It therefore appears that the notion of capacity
to make a will is related to the general notion of capacity found in Articles
153 to 297 C.C.Q.
[47]
Articles 153 and 154 C.C.Q. provide as follows:

153.
Full
age or the age of majority is 18 years.

On attaining full age, a person
ceases to be a minor and has the full exercise of all his civil rights.

154.
In
no case may the capacity of a person of full age be limited except by express
provision of law or by a judgment ordering the institution of protective
supervision.

[
75
]

Because the mother was over 18 years old and
there is no judgment ordering the institution of protective supervision in
relation to her, she had legal capacity at all relevant times. She therefore
had capacity to make a will.

[
76
]

That does not end the inquiry. The usual defects
in consent apply in the case of a will. Article 1399 C.C.Q. provides:

1399.
Consent must be free and enlightened.

It may be vitiated by error, fear or
lesion.

[
77
]

Article 831 of the previous
Civil Code of
Lower Canada
provided as follows:

831.

Every person of
full age,
of sound intellect
, and capable of alienating his property,
may dispose of it freely by will, without distinction as to its origin or
nature, either in favour of his consort, or of one or more of his children, or
of any other person capable of acquiring and possessing, and without reserve,
restriction, or limitation; saving the prohibitions, restrictions, and causes
of nullity mentioned in this code, and all dispositions and conditions contrary
to public order or good morals.

(Emphasis added)

[
78
]

The notion of “sound intellect”, or “sain
d’esprit” in the French version, is not mentioned in the
Civil Code of
Québec
. However, the courts have continued to apply the criteria developed
with respect to “sound intellect” in their analysis of capacity to execute a
will.
[48]
It is not clear whether “sound intellect”
forms part of the required capacity to make a will, or whether it is related to
the validity of the consent given. It is not necessary for purposes of the
present case to decide that issue.

[
79
]

Beaulne defines the relevant test as follows:

La capacité d’une personne d’apprécier
la portée et les conséquences du testament qu’elle s’apprête à signer, ainsi
que sa compréhension du sens et de la portée des dispositions contenues à
l’acte et de s’y arrêter volontairement ….
[49]

[
80
]

The authors and the courts make the following
statements about the test :
[50]

•

A person can be of unsound intellect without
being insane;

•

Old age is not sufficient to establish that the
person is of unsound intellect;

•

Alzheimer’s disease may cause a person to be of
unsound intellect, but it is not an automatic conclusion;

•

A person of sound mind can make, modify or annul
a will right up until his or her death;
[51]

•

Frequent changes to the will do not establish
unsoundness of mind; and

•

The reasonableness or unreasonableness of the
testamentary dispositions may be an element in assessing the soundness of the
testator’s intellect, but it is not conclusive.

[
81
]

Moreover, the courts have held that there is a
presumption that every person is of sound intellect.
[52]
As
a result, the burden of proving that the testator was not of sound intellect
falls on the party contesting the validity of the will. However, the Court of
Appeal held that if the party contesting the will establishes generally that
the testator was not of sound intellect, the burden shifts to the party
defending the will to demonstrate that the will was executed during a lucid
interval:

[42]       En matière de capacité
de tester, le principe cardinal est que le fardeau de prouver l’incapacité
incombe au plaideur qui demande la nullité de l’acte puisque chacun est présumé
être sain d’esprit. Ainsi, au stade initial, la partie qui requiert
l’annulation du testament doit mettre en doute, de façon générale, la capacité
de tester : « Il suffirait à ce stade, de prouver l’existence d’un
état habituel d’aliénation ou de faiblesse d’esprit. Faute de prouver l’état
habituel d’insanité, le recours en annulation du testament échouera et la
validité de celui-ci sera reconnu ».

[43]       Si cette capacité est
sérieusement mise en doute par une preuve prima facie, le fardeau de la preuve
se déplace sur celui qui prétend à la validité de l’acte. Il reviendra alors à
ce dernier de démontrer la capacité de tester lors de la confection du
testament. Bien que cela puisse s’avérer un exercice ardu, il faudra démontrer
un intervalle de lucidité, même dans une situation générale d’affaiblissement
mental. Ainsi, une contre-preuve convaincante amènera la validité du testament.
[53]

[
82
]

With respect to the evidence admissible to prove
the testator’s state of mind, Beaulne states the following :

373
.
–
Les moyens de preuve
. – La difficulté du procès en annulation de
testament pour absence de volonté de la part du testateur porte généralement
sur des questions de preuve. Ce qu’il faut prouver essentiellement en l’occurrence,
c’est l’absence de consentement de la part du testateur au moment où le
testament a été fait. Comme cette preuve ne peut résulter du testament même –
sous réserve du cas où les dispositions en sont incohérentes -, on admet
qu’elle puisse être apportée par tous moyens, même par des circonstances
extrinsèques. Les moyens les plus usuels sont l’expertise médicale, plus
particulièrement l’expertise psychiatrique, les autres écrits émanant du
testateur, les témoignages des personnes qui ont été en contact avec lui à
l’époque de la confection du testament.
[54]

[

following conclusions:

•

Expert evidence tends to be quite important in
these matters;
[55]

•

The evidence of doctors and other medical
professionals who treated the testator is also important;

•

The evidence of ordinary witnesses who had
contact with the testator in the relevant period is admissible and can be
important, particularly when there is a conflict among the experts;
[56]

•

The evidence of the notary is admissible but is
not conclusive. It has the same value as the testimony of an ordinary witness.
Further, the statement in the will that the testator is of sound mind does not
need to be contested under Article 258 of the
Code of Civil Procedure

because the notary does not have the duty to ascertain the testator’s soundness
of mind;

2.

Legal test for undue influence

[
84
]

Teresa also pleads that the mother was unduly
influenced by the siblings with the result that the wills do not reflect her
true intention.

[
85
]

The courts have defined undue influence as
follows:

[58]

Une lecture de plusieurs jugements en matière de
captation permet de retenir que la captation est une manière d'agir qui peut
comporter un ensemble de manœuvres que l'on peut qualifier de dolosives dont la
ruse, les pressions indues et tromperies, visant à influencer une personne et
en la maintenant dans un état de dépendance afin de lui soutirer un
consentement et pour l’octroi d’un don ou d'un legs auquel elle n’aurait
peut-être pas donné son assentiment n’eut été de ce comportement répréhensible
du bénéficiaire.
[59]

[
86
]

It is not sufficient to show that the beneficiary
curried favour with the testator or made suggestions or gave advice to the
testator in the hope of being made a legatee. It must go beyond that into
notions of “manoeuvres … dolosives” – intercepting the mail, isolating the
testator and denigrating other family members and friends.
[60]

[
87
]

Moreover, the undue influence must be the cause
of the testamentary disposition.
[61]

[
88
]

The burden of proof is on the person alleging
undue influence. There is no shifting of the burden of proof.
[62]

[
89
]

It is a difficult burden to meet because the
person alleging undue influence typically is not present and is not able to
testify as to what happened. The court will generally be asked to draw
inferences from facts such as the testator not being strong physically or
mentally, the defendant cutting the testator off from family and friends
including the plaintiff, the testator being brought to the notary by the
defendant or the notary receiving instructions from the defendant, or the
testator making drastic changes to the will over a short period of time which
do not appear rational and which favour the defendant to the detriment of the
plaintiff.
[63]
Further, the efforts to conceal undue influence may themselves be
proof of undue influence.
[64]

[
90
]

However, the person alleging undue influence
must put forward more than “un simple soupçon ou hypothèse” and “les
allegations, très vagues”.
[65]

[
91
]

There is an overlap between undue influence and
incapacity, in that a testator who is in a weakened state will be less able to
resist any undue influence. As a result, they can be pleaded together:

Les comportements qui permettent de
conclure à captation varieront en fonction des circonstances particulières de
chaque dossier. L’âge, l’état de santé et la condition sociale du testateur
jouent un rôle important dans le degré de résistance que peut opposer ce
dernier envers un comportement dolosif. Le degré de résistance est d’ailleurs
en lui-même un indice sérieux pour conclure à captation. Pour cette raison, il
est fréquent que le testament soit attaqué à la fois pour captation et pour
insanité, les deux arguments étant tout à fait compatibles et pouvant être
cumulés.
[66]

4.

Hearsay objections

[
126
]

A number of witnesses testified as to what they
had been told by others, most notably what they had been told by the mother
about her wills and her relationship with her children. Objections were made on
both sides.

[
127
]

In order to avoid the need to repeat the
objections and have a debate each time this happened, the Court adopted the
following approach:

•

The Court presumed that the evidence of the
statement being made is admissible to prove that the statement was made and no
more;

•

The Court presumed that the other party objects
to the evidence being used to prove that the statement was true;

•

The Court took such objections under reserve;

•

If a party wishes to rely on the evidence of the
statement being made as evidence that the statement was true, it must raise the
argument in its closing argument; and

•

If no such argument is raised in the closing
arguments, then the Court will limit its use of the evidence to proof that the
statement was made and no more.

[
128
]

The argument was raised in the closing
arguments.

[
129
]

As a starting point, the Court notes that the
purpose of making this evidence is to prove not that the statements were made
but that they are true. As a result, this is in principle covered by the
hearsay rule.

[
130
]

Articles 2870 and 2871 C.C.Q. codify the
exceptions to the hearsay rule:

2870.
A
statement made by a person who does not appear as a
witness
,
concerning facts to which he could have legally testified
,
is admissible as testimony on application and after notice is given to the
adverse party, provided the court authorizes it.

The court shall, however, ascertain
that it is
impossible for the declarant to appear as a witness, or that it
is unreasonable to require him to do so
, and that
the reliability of the
statement is sufficiently guaranteed by the circumstances in which it is made
.

Reliability is presumed to be
sufficiently guaranteed with respect in particular to documents drawn up in the
ordinary course of business of an enterprise, to documents entered in a
register required by law to be kept, and spontaneous statements that are
contemporaneous to the occurrence of the facts.

2871.
Previous statements by a person who appears as a witness,
concerning facts to which he may legally testify, are admissible as testimony
if their reliability is sufficiently guaranteed.

(Emphasis added)

[
131
]

Most of the testimony at issue involved
witnesses testifying as to statements made by the mother about her will or
about her relationship with her children.

[
132
]

Clearly, it is impossible for the mother to
testify at the trial. The first condition under Article 2870 C.C.Q. is
therefore met.

[
133
]

The second condition is whether the reliability
of the statement is sufficiently guaranteed by the circumstances in which it is
made. The Defendants have produced a number of cases which suggest that this
test is met when the witness repeating the statements is a disinterested third
party, but not when the witness is interested in the outcome of the litigation.
[79]

[
134
]

With respect, this is not the proper analysis.
There are two statements: the original statement by the declarant, and the
statement by the witness repeating what the declarant said. When Article 2870
C.C.Q. refers to the circumstantial guarantees of reliability of the statement,
it is referring to the original statement by the declarant. As stated by the
Supreme Court, the focus is on the reliability of the declarant:

If a statement sought to be adduced
by way of hearsay evidence is made under circumstances which substantially
negate the possibility that
the declarant
was untruthful or mistaken,
the hearsay evidence may be said to be "reliable", i.e., a
circumstantial guarantee of trustworthiness is established.
[80]

(Emphasis added)

[
135
]

As a result, the admissibility of the hearsay
evidence does not depend on the witness testifying as to the hearsay statement.
It is possible that the witnesses were not remembering correctly or were lying
when they repeated the mother’s statements. Some witnesses had an interest to
lie while others did not. Those matters can be explored in cross-examination of
the witness and the Court will consider all of those matters in assessing the
credibility of the witness. However, the credibility of the witness goes to the
weight of his or her evidence, not its admissibility.
[81]

[
136
]

As for the circumstantial guarantees of
reliability of the mother’s statements, most of the statements at issue were
made spontaneously and contemporaneously in circumstances where it is unlikely
that she was mistaken or lying. Further, the mother had nothing to gain or to
lose by lying about her will or about her relationship with her children.

[
137
]

As a result, the Court concludes that the
testimony with respect to various statements made by the mother is admissible.
The weight to be given to the evidence depends on the credibility of the
witness testifying with respect to the mother’s statement.

[
138
]

Some witnesses also testified about statements
made by the children. Those statements fall into two categories. The first
category is statements in the declarant’s interest. Those statements do not
have a circumstantial guarantee of trustworthiness because the declarant had an
interest in the statement. In any event, the evidence is unnecessary because
all of the children testified and had the opportunity to testify as to those
statements or to their content.

[
139
]

The second category is statements against the
declarant’s interest. The common law has always had an exception to the hearsay
rule with respect to declarations against interest, because they have greater
guarantees of trustworthiness: the declarant had no interest in saying it and
would not have said it if it was not true. Those statements are therefore
admissible. Again, because the children all testified, they had the opportunity
to explain or deny any statements attributed to them by another witness.

6.

Analysis of the evidence on capacity

[
208
]

Teresa raises lack of capacity as a subsidiary
argument to the principal argument of undue influence. However, it is useful to
examine the question of capacity first because a mental impairment that is not
sufficient to result in a finding of incapacity may be a relevant factor in the
undue influence analysis.

[
209
]

On the issue of capacity, there are three types
of evidence: direct evidence of persons who saw the mother during this time,
expert evidence, and circumstantial evidence based principally on the contents
of the wills and codicils. The Court will review the direct evidence in roughly
chronological order divided into three periods: prior to March 2009, March to
May 2009 and after May 2009. The Court will then consider the expert evidence.
The Court will consider the circumstantial evidence in the next section of the
judgment dealing with undue influence.

a.

Prior to March 2009

[
210
]

Three doctors who treated the mother prior to
March 2009 testified:

•

Dr. Krasny, a rheumatologist who had the mother
as a patient for 5 to 10 years;

•

Dr. Lazarus, a doctor in family medicine who
followed the mother from the mid 1980s until January 2009; and

•

Dr. Davis, a psychiatrist specializing in

[

]

files, but they remembered the mother. They recalled a variety of physical

because of a stroke she had suffered in 2004. In his notes, he stated:

significant dementia (depression is presenting issue) but her orientation, intelligence

[102]

213

[103]

214
]

He saw her periodically after that until April 8, 2009. He found that she was

215
]

d’indices pouvant nous laisser soupçonner la présence de pertes cognitives.”

[
216
]

Alan Huang, who saw the mother on November 10, 2008 at the Royal Victoria

but ne did not recommend any follow-up.

217
]

218

b.

[
219
]

Fortin was the social worker from the CLSC
assigned to the mother and the father. She testified that the file had been
opened with the CLSC for at least ten years prior to April 2009.

[
220
]

Fortin testified about the family meeting on
March 10, 2009 and the events leading up to the motion for psychiatric
evaluation on April 23, 2009.

[
221
]

In her testimony, Fortin said that she called
the March 10, 2009 meeting because she was concerned about the mother and her
ability to look after herself. These concerns intensified over the next six
weeks when Teresa cancelled the CLSC services and Jadwiga told her about the
mother being cut off from the siblings. Fortin ultimately set a date to visit
the mother, and when the mother was not home that day she made the motion for a
psychiatric evaluation.

[
222
]

The Court finds that her evidence on these
issues is credible. However, on the same date as the motion, Fortin drafted a
report for her successor in the file.
[107]
In
her report, she said that Teresa had isolated the mother from the siblings. She
referred to certain financial issues and the possibility that Teresa was taking
advantage of the mother. She even wrote that she suspected that Teresa had “un
certain problème de personalité”. In her cross-examination, Fortin acknowledged
various errors in her report and in the motion for a psychiatric evaluation. She
also acknowledged that some of these allegations were not to her personal
knowledge but had come from the siblings.

[
223
]

The Court will not give weight to those
allegations.

[
224
]

However, the more serious issue relates to the
allegations in the motion.

[
225
]

In the motion for a psychiatric evaluation, she alleges “la
détérioration de son état mental” and “Nous questionnons son jugement et son
discernement”. The motion also alleges “Un mauvais jugement relié à la
résistance à l’aide, à son incapacité de mobiliser de l’aide puis qu’elle a
fait débrancher le téléphone”. Teresa is not even mentioned in the motion.
[108]

[
226
]

There are also the notes of Chantal Coderre of a call with Fortin on
the same date as the motion. In her notes, Coderre states that Fortin told her
that the mother is alert, oriented in the three spheres, communicates well, and
has adequate judgment and self-awareness.
[109]

[
227
]

There is a blatant inconsistency between these
contemporaneous documents. The Court can only conclude that Fortin did not have
any basis for the allegations of deterioration of the mother’s mental state and
poor judgment. It appears that she only made these allegations because she was
concerned about the mother and wanted to get her out of the house, and the
motion for a psychiatric evaluation was the easiest way to do it. She therefore
alleged the elements necessary to get the order without regard to their truth.

[
228
]

The Court will not give any weight to those
allegations either.

[
229
]

The mother saw Dr. Davis for the last time on
April 8, 2009, one month after her husband had died.
[110]

Contrary to what Teresa alleged, he found that she was coping well. Teresa
complained to him that other family members were trying to place the mother in
a home immediately, and she wanted legal help to prevent it. He recommended
that she get a notary or a lawyer. He also recommended a MMSE test. Her score
was 17/28,
[111]
which he seems to have considered sufficient for her to go see the
notary. He testified that a change of two points in three years was quite
random and indicated that she was stable.

[
230
]

The Defendants produced notes by two doctors who
saw the mother while she was at Hôpital Notre-Dame:

•

Dr. André Gamache was a psychiatrist. He saw the
mother on April 24, 2009 to assess her mental state. He administered a MMSE

and there was a language barrier that prevented her from doing others). He
concluded that she was going through normal mourning.
[112]

•

Dr. Catherine Beauregard had long meetings with
the mother between April 27 and 30, 2009. In her report, she concluded that the
mother’s cognitive functions were “globalement normales” and that although the
mother’s judgment had been questioned (possibly by Fortin in the motion) she

problems were due to normal mourning and anxiety caused by the conflict within
the family.
[113]

•

Christine Legault, an ergotherapist, prepared a lengthy
report on April 29 in which she concluded “[patiente est] capable de prendre
des décisions appropriées la concernant si toutes les informations pertinentes
à la prise de décision lui sont présentées de façon claire + ordonnée.”
[114]

•

Benoît-LeBlanc completed the “Demande de
services inter-établissements” on May 1 and 5, 2009 in which he noted no mental
incapacity (May 1, p. 2), and that the patient was “orienté dans les 3 sphères
T E P” (May 5, p. 3).
[115]

•

Nadeau’s notes state that the mother was “apte”
in early May 2009, without more detail. Nadeau evaluated the mother’s autonomy

[116]

[
231
]

and May 2009 and was satisfied that she had testamentary capacity.

[
