e
.
Expert evidence

i.

Dr. Ruby Friedman

[
250
]

Dr. Friedman is the Site Director of Geriatric
Medicine at the Jewish General Hospital. The court declared him an expert in
geriatric medicine, dementia in the elderly, issues of competency in the
elderly, and drug treatments related thereto. He was recognized as an expert
and gave his opinion on mental capacity or incapacity in several other matters.
He produced a report dated July 4, 2013.

[
251
]

In his report, he stated “I have several
concerns related to her mental capacities” during the time frame from March
2009 to March 2010, based on her low MMSE and CASE scores, Dr. Davis’s
diagnosis of major depression in April 2006, Dr. Huang’s assessment in November
2008, and Fortin’s comments questioning the mother’s judgment and behaviour
leading up to the motion in April 2009.
[133]

[
252
]

He concluded as follows:

In summary, on the basis of the
history of major depression since 2006, and repeatedly abnormal cognitive
testing since November 2008, Mrs. Taperek’s competency to sign or consent to
multiple wills can be seriously questioned.
[134]

[
253
]

Dr. Friedman’s testimony focused largely on the mother’s
performance on her MMSE test scores. The MMSE is a screening test designed to
measure cognitive impairment. It is typically scored out of 30, with a score of
26 or lower suggesting some minor form of cognitive deficit.

[
254
]

However, Dr. Friedman cautioned against putting
too much weight on an MMSE score itself. He testified that the MMSE is a
screening test and not a test of mental competency. A person could score a
perfect 30 and still suffer from a cognitive impairment. Conversely, a person
with a low score may not actually suffer from any impairment. He emphasized the
necessity of careful scrutiny of each exam in order to see where the points
were lost.

[
255
]

Test results might also be affected upwards or
downwards by improper administration of the test. Further, factors such as
distractions and language can lead to low results, and that coaching or the
learning effect can lead to high results. He also suggested that medication can
affect the results.

[
256
]

Dr. Friedman expressed concern at the mother’s
repeatedly low scores on the MMSE. The mother received a score of 16 on
multiple occasions, although many of these scores were not out of 30. In many
administrations of the test, sections of the MMSE were not scored at all on
account of the mother’s cultural and educational background.

[
257
]

Dr. Friedman considered the extreme fluctuations
in the mother’s MMSE scores to be anomalous. He said that a variation of a
couple of points would be normal. In five of the seven tests, her scores declined
from 19 to 16 from 2006 to 2010, with a varying number of questions omitted. On
the other two tests, she scored 29/30 and 26-27/30. It is noteworthy that her
score of 26-27 was achieved on her last test, in March 2010. Dr. Friedman
stated that such fluctuations are extremely unlikely, and that he had never
seen such improvements in his 28 years of practice.

[
258
]

Dr. Friedman highlighted a correlation between
the two higher scores and the administrators of those tests. The scores of 26-27
and 29 were achieved on MMSE tests administered by family doctors, while the
low scores were administered by health care professionals that he considered to
be more experienced in dealing with cognitive functioning in the elderly such
as psychiatrists, geriatric specialists and ergotherapists. He suggested that
some family doctors may be tempted to help their patients achieve higher scores
by prompting them with hints to the correct answers.

[
259
]

He concluded that the higher MMSE scores of 26-27
and 29 should be disregarded as invalid.

[
260
]

Dr. Friedman also expressed concern regarding
the mother’s performance on the CASE test, characterizing her score of 55.5/96
as “abnormally low” and “worrisome”. Like the MMSE, the CASE is also a
screening test, although it is considerably more difficult, lengthy and
sensitive to impairment relative to the MMSE. This test noted deficits in the mother’s
attention, concentration, immediate recall, and calculation.

[
261
]

According to Dr. Friedman, the mother’s
repeatedly poor performance in her mental evaluations between June 28, 2006 and
March 24, 2010 should have led to follow-up testing in order to determine her
degree of cognitive impairment and whether or not she suffered from any mental
disorders, such as dementia or Alzheimer’s.

ii.    Dr. Isabelle Collin

[
262
]

Dr. Isabelle Collin has a Ph.D. in
neuropsychology and runs a private practice. She previously worked for 15 years
in a hospital setting. In her practice, she regularly works with patients
suffering from Alzheimer’s disease and symptoms of dementia. She regularly
administers and interprets psychometric tests. This was the first time she had
appeared in Court as an expert witness. The Court declared her an expert in the
cognitive evaluation of the elderly. She produced a report on March 21, 2014 on
behalf of the Defendants.
[135]

[
263
]

Her review focused on the medical notes and
social service notes of the health care professionals and caseworkers who
interacted with the mother, including her performance on various MMSE and CASE
tests.

[
264
]

Her report concludes as follows:

Suite à l’analyse du type d’erreurs
relevées aux tests cognitifs, nous doutons que les difficultés cognitives de
madame Konysz aient été de nature et d’ampleur suffisante pour nuire à sa
capacité à déterminer ses dernières volontés, en 2009 aussi bien qu’en 2010. Ainsi,
nous sommes en désaccord avec les conclusions du docteur Friedman à l’effet que
l’aptitude de Madame Konysz à déterminer ses dernières volontés en 2009 et 2010
puisse être sérieusement mise en doute.
[136]

[
265
]

Dr. Collin agreed with Dr. Friedman that the
mother performed abnormally low on many of her tests. However, she disagreed
that these scores have any bearing on the mother’s capacity to amend her will
during the relevant time period. Dr. Collin emphasized that the MMSE and CASE
are both screening tools for detecting cognitive impairment. She agreed with
Dr. Friedman that it was important to see which questions were missed. For
example, the mother consistently failed to answer the math questions. According
to Dr. Collin, it is inappropriate to draw inferences from these tests about a
person’s mental capacity to make autonomous and reasoned decisions.

[
266
]

Dr. Collin considered it more significant that
none of the health care professionals who administered these tests recommended
follow-up testing. She inferred from this fact that they were not especially
worried about her mental capacity. In contrast with Dr. Friedman, Dr. Collin
does not see any reason to consider that the test administrators were mistaken.
Rather, she deferred to their judgment, and noted that they were all, family
doctors included, well-qualified to administer and interpret these tests.
Regarding the low MMSE scores and the anomalous fluctuations in those scores,
Dr. Collin cited linguistic and cultural barriers, a lack of education,
physical pain, depression, stress related to her grief and to the family
dispute, as well as the pharmacological effects of certain medications as
possible explanatory factors.

[
267
]

Much of Dr. Collin’s analysis focused on the
notes of the various social workers and health care professionals who
interacted with the mother rather than the MMSE and CASE scores. While these
notes often made mention of the mother’s depressed mood and state of anxiety
relating to her family dispute, as well as occasional mention of a partial
state of disorientation, they did not call into question her capacity or her judgment.
Regarding the note in April 2009 by Dr. Davis’s nurse stating a need for
further testing, Dr. Collin clarified that this note was made in the context of
a request by Teresa in order to assess the mother’s capacity to make a will. It
was not indicative of a concern with the mother’s general state of mind.
Regarding Fortin’s questioning of the mother’s judgment, it was subsequently
made clear that Teresa was responsible for the actions that caused Fortin to
doubt the mother, such as changing the locks and disconnecting the telephone.

[
268
]

Dr. Collin considered the April 2009 report of the
ergotherapist to be the most informative indicator of the mother’s
decision-making capacity. The ergotherapist noted that the mother was partially
disoriented in time and had attentional deficits, such as an inability to multitask.
However, she also observed that the mother was able to persevere in
accomplishing a task, operating a microwave for example, without losing track
and she was able to correct her own mistakes. The ergotherapist concluded that
the mother was capable of making appropriate decisions as long as the relevant
information was clearly presented to her.

[
269
]

Dr. Collin concluded that while the mother
likely presented certain cognitive deficits relating to her working memory and
orientation, as well as physical pain and emotional stress, she maintained her
capacity to critically analyze her situation and make autonomous judgments
throughout the time period during which she was amending her will.

iii.   Analysis of the expert evidence

[
270
]

Both experts reviewed the mother’s MMSE and CASE
scores.

[
271
]

With respect to two higher MMSE test scores of
29 and 26-27 out of 30, the Court accepts the evidence of Dr. Friedman that
those two scores are anomalous and unrepresentative of the mother’s performance
on the tests. Both were administered by family doctors who had less experience
administering tests of that nature. The Court will exclude those two test
results. As a result, The MMSE test scores show a downwards pattern, from 19/28
on July 19, 2006 to 16/30 on February 11, 2010. These results are consistent
and show some degree of mental impairment which is worsening over time. The
CASE test results point to the same conclusion.

[
272
]

In this context, Teresa points to the decision
in
Bertrand
. In that case, the testator had scored 23/30 on a MMSE test,
which the expert said “peut constituer un indice de démence”.
[137]
He was also suffering from “un trouble vasculaire”.
[138]
The Court concluded that he was incapable.

[
273
]

However, the MMSE test score was not conclusive
or even relevant in the final analysis. He testator wrote the test five years
before he passed away. Two years later, his score was 28/30. His mental
condition deteriorated significantly in the last year of his life:

[64]       Il me semble évident que
M. Bertrand était un homme perturbé, ayant des difficultés à contenir ses
émotions et ressentant une agressivité et une colère exacerbées comparativement
à la moyenne des gens, et ce, en raison de ses troubles cérébro-vasculaires
[21]
.  Son comportement et sa personnalité se sont
transformés à la suite de ces accidents cérébro-vasculaires.  Le D
r
Pomerleau
le reconnaît   clairement :

[…]

[65]

La fréquence des manifestations de ce comportement agressif a
nettement augmenté dans les mois qui ont précédé la confection du testament en
cause.  Le rapport du D
r
Bernard Ménard les note :

[…]
[139]

[
274
]

In another case cited by Teresa, the Court found
that the testator was not of sound mind even though his MMSE scores were 29/30
and 30/30.
[140]

[
275
]

Both experts agreed that the MMSE and the CASE
are only screening tests and that it is not appropriate to draw any conclusions
based solely on the test results. Dr. Friedman suggested that these test
results raise doubts as to the mother’s capacity and indicated the need for
follow-up testing to come to a clear conclusion.

[
276
]

The Court cannot conclude on the basis of the
MMSE and CASE test results alone that the mother lacked the capacity to make a
valid will. Moreover, when assessed as a whole, Dr. Friedman’s opinion and
testimony do not in themselves establish that the mother lacked the mental
capacity to amend her will at any point prior to her death. Dr. Friedman merely
concludes that he has concerns as to her capacity and that follow-up was
necessary. In the absence of any follow-up, the Court cannot conclude that the
mother lacked capacity.

[
277
]

Dr. Collin takes this point further. She points
to the lack of further testing as indicative that the professionals who
conducted the various tests considered that no follow-up was necessary because
they had no doubts about the mother’s capacity. The Court is not prepared to
draw that conclusion. It appears that further testing would have been
appropriate to evaluate the mother’s capacity but that no one did any follow-up
because no one perceived any need to come to a conclusion on the mother’s capacity.
It is telling that when Teresa asked Dr. Davis for an opinion on the mother’s
capacity, he immediately indicated that further test would be required before
he could give an opinion.

f.

Conclusion

[
278
]

None of the professionals ever concluded that
the mother lacked capacity and only one, Dr. Huang in November 2008, even
suggested the possibility of cognitive impairment. Dr. Davis diagnosed a major
depression in 2006, but he noted progress between 2006 and 2009. Both the
social worker and the ergotherapist concluded that the mother possessed sound
judgment despite her cognitive impairments.

[
279
]

It is also relevant to consider the testimony of
the two notaries, each of whom explained the wills to the mother and was
satisfied that she understood.

[
280
]

MacDonald also testified that he saw the mother
eight to ten times at Bercy in 2009-2010 and that she participated fully in the
conversations and understood everything when they talked.

[
281
]

The circumstances are very similar to those in
McDermid

c.
Howman-
Trainor
, where the Court held that the testatrix, who
disinherited her husband of 47 years, was of sound mind: conflicting expert
evidence, medical file with no finding of confusion or dementia, and lay
evidence from friends, relatives and the notary. The Court stated:

[31]

Close friends and relatives of the deceased have testified that the
deceased was fully cognizant in July 1997. Not only was she aware of what she
was doing, she was steadfast in her determination to alter her Will because she
had had a genuine change of heart about her husband's character.

[32]

This is a case where there is no lack of medical evidence. The
deceased had a complicated medical history and was well attended by
disinterested medical professional. For this reason, in analyzing the
deceased's competence or incompetence at the time of her new Will, the Court
will focus on the content of her medical file.

[…]

[37]

The evidence establishes that the nurses kept notes and that their
training requires them to make a note of a state of confusion, or delirium, or
incoherence, in a patient. From her admission to Pierrefonds Manor in May 1997
until her departure in July, there is not a single mention of any such episode
in the notes of the nurses.

[…]

[39]

In 1997, the general practitioner who had attended to Mrs McDermid
retired and he referred her to another general practitioner. The deceased
consulted the latter four times over the summer of 1997. The referral form
indicates that she was then lucid - and very intelligent. Her new physician
testified that he found no sign of paranoia, no cognitive deficiency, nothing
to indicate mental incompetence. The deceased's complaints had to do with being
unhappy in the nursing care facility and having a difficult matrimonial situation,
and also with pain and tiredness. She exhibited no confusion or dementia to a
doctor of medicine well versed in recognizing such traits.

[40]

This matches the impression of close friends and relatives who found
the deceased to be completely lucid and capable over the same period of time.
It also matches that of third parties who dealt with the deceased in other
professional capacities: the notary, who testified that the deceased was very
clear as to what she wanted to do, the bank and trust employees as well as the
nursing staff retained by the deceased.

[…]

[42]

Finally, a brief mention must be made of the expert medical
evidence.

[43]

Neither expert had ever met the deceased and both opinions are based
on their interpretation of the medical file.

[…]

[45]

[Plaintiff’s expert’s] opinion, simply put, does not accord with the
rest of the evidence, and his interpretation of the medical file paints a much
darker picture than do the physicians who attended Mrs McDermid at the time and
whose testimony is in the record.

[…]

[47]

[Defendant’s expert’s opinion] is an opinion which accords well with
the rest of the evidence and the Court accepts it.
[141]

[
282
]

In all of these circumstances, the Court is
satisfied that the direct evidence and the expert evidence does not establish
on the balance of probabilities that the mother lacked capacity to make a valid
will.

[
283
]

However, the Court is satisfied that the direct
evidence and the expert evidence demonstrates that the mother had some degree
of mental impairment falling short of incapacity to make a valid will.

7.

Analysis and Conclusion on Undue
Influence

[
284
]

The principal argument put forward by Teresa for
annulling the wills made between March 2009 and March 2010 is that the wills do
not reflect the mother’s free will because she was being unduly influenced by
the siblings.

[
285
]

As is often the case in this sort of matter,
Teresa does not have any direct evidence of undue influence. Essentially, she
asks the Court to presume that there was undue influence in the absence of any
direct proof on the basis that (1) the siblings had the opportunity to
influence the mother against Teresa because the mother was isolated from
Teresa, and (2) the wills and the December 28, 2009 letter can only be
explained by the exercise of undue influence.

a.   Opportunity

[
286
]

One very important factor in considering
Teresa’s claim of undue influence is whether the siblings had the opportunity
to exercise undue influence over the mother.

[
287
]

The evidence is clear that Teresa had little
contact with the mother after April 24, 2009. Teresa saw the mother at least
once at Hôpital Notre-Dame and at least once at the Jewish Elder Care. Teresa
did not see the mother at Nazaire-Piché until a couple of days before the
mother passed away. In addition, Teresa saw the mother during the mother’s
visits to Bercy and at the Courthouse and the Régie du logement during the
various legal proceedings. These encounters were all quite brief.

[
288
]

The evidence also establishes that the mother did
not want to see Teresa.

[
289
]

The siblings were involved. They instructed the
staff at Jewish Elder Care and Nazaire-Piché that the mother did not want to
see Teresa and they gave the staff a picture of Teresa to ensure that these
instructions would be followed.
[142]

They refused to tell Teresa that the mother was at Nazaire-Piché. The siblings
say that they were following the mother’s instructions. Martin said that at
Nazaire-Piché they encourage family contacts and do not accept instructions of
this nature from a sibling, but in this case it was clear to them that the
mother did not want any contact with Teresa.

[
290
]

It is important to understand why the mother did
not want to see Teresa, and in particular whether it is because the siblings
turned the mother against her.

[
291
]

The relationship between Teresa and her mother
prior to April 2009 appears to be normal. Dr. Lazarus qualified the
relationship between Teresa and the parents as very close.

[
292
]

However, the relationship deteriorated because
of the events in April 2009. The Court finds that Teresa attempted to cut the
mother off from the siblings.

[
293
]

Teresa argues that she did not keep the mother
as a prisoner in her own home. She says that the mother was not a prisoner but
went out. She explains that she changed the locks because the siblings were
taking things, and that she unplugged the telephone and then changed the number
because the siblings were harassing the mother to force her to move to a
nursing home. She adds that when the police came and when Jadwiga and Donna saw
the mother in April 2009, the mother did not want to go with them.

[
294
]

It is possible that Teresa was acting in good
faith in an attempt to protect the mother. However, that does not matter. What
matters is how the mother perceived it, and whether it caused her to become
angry with Teresa. The evidence suggests that the attempt to cut the mother off
from the siblings is the basis for the mother’s feelings of anger towards
Teresa.

[
295
]

Within a few days of her being taken to Hôpital
Notre-Dame, the mother became angry with Teresa for what Teresa had done and
said that she did not want to see Teresa.

[
296
]

There is confirmation of this from Teresa and
from third parties during the period that the mother was at Hôpital Notre-Dame:

•

Teresa testified that the mother called her from
the hospital at lunch time on April 24, but when Teresa called back in the
evening, the nurse told her that the mother did not want to speak to her;

•

On April 27, the mother told Dr. Beauregard that
she did not understand why Teresa cut the telephone and changed the locks;
[143]

•

Teresa went to the hospital on April 28. The
head nurse went to see the mother and then told Teresa that the mother did not
want to see her, and security guards escorted Teresa out of the building;
[144]

•

The mother confirmed to Dr. Beauregard on April
29 that she did not want to see Teresa;
[145]

•

At the family meeting on April 30, the mother
said that she did not want to go home with Teresa and she did not want Teresa
to take her out on May 3;

•

When Teresa went to the hospital to take the
mother out on May 3, the mother said that she was not going out and when Teresa
insisted, the nurse told her to leave;

•

Benoît-Leblanc and Nadeau also noted the
conflict with Teresa in their reports.
[146]

[
297
]

The situation did not change while the mother
was at the Jewish Elder Care or at Nazaire-Piché. She did not want to see or
talk to Teresa. She was sad when she talked about Teresa. This is confirmed by
the testimony of Martin and Tanguay.

[
298
]

The mother also saw Teresa at Bercy, the
Courthouse and the Régie du logement. MacDonald testified that the mother did
not want Teresa to come in to her home on Bercy because she said that she did
not trust her and was afraid of her. When Teresa asked her lawyer to deliver a
letter to the mother at the Courthouse, the mother refused to take it. The
mother and Teresa exchanged angry words at the Régie du logement.

[
299
]

Finally, the mother explained her feelings about
Teresa to the notaries when she was alone with them.

[
300
]

On the other hand, Teresa testified that on the
few occasions when she saw the mother after April 2009, the mother was always
happy to see her. This is not credible. The weight of the evidence, mostly from
the siblings but also from MacDonald, is that the meetings between the mother
and Teresa during this period were brief and tense. The evidence establishes
that the mother did not want to see Teresa, principally because of the events
of April 2009.

[
301
]

To all of this, Teresa answers that if the
mother did not want to see her, it is because the siblings poisoned the
mother’s mind towards Teresa.

[
302
]

This appears unlikely. The mother started saying
these things to the doctors and social workers within a week of arriving at
Hôpital Notre-Dame. This suggests that it is a true expression of her feelings
and not the result of influence by the siblings. Moreover, the mother’s
attitude towards Teresa was the same when the siblings were there and when they
were not, and the mother never telephoned Teresa in her time at Nazaire-Piché.
This again tends to suggest that she was not being influenced.

[
303
]

Further, this is not a case where the mother was
constantly in the presence of the siblings and was cut off from the outside
world. The siblings visited her on almost a daily basis, but they were not
always with her. She saw other people. She was in daily contact with the other
residents and the staff of the three institutions without the siblings being
around. She saw doctors and social workers. She saw the notaries and spent time
with them alone. She spent time alone with MacDonald. She had a telephone in
her rooms at the Jewish Elder Care and Nazaire-Piché and she could have called
anyone at any time. She could have called Teresa, but she did not.

[
304
]

The Court therefore concludes that the siblings
had the opportunity to turn the mother against Teresa in the sense that they
saw her and Teresa did not. However, there are reasons why the mother did not
want to see Teresa, and the circumstances surrounding this opportunity are not
such as to give rise to a presumption that the siblings exercised the opportunity.

b.   Content of the will and the letter as proof of undue influence
and incapacity

[
305
]

Finally, with no direct proof of the siblings
exerting pressure on the mother, Teresa pleads that the contents of the wills
and the letter dated December 28, 2009 can only be explained by the exercise of
undue influence or the mother’s incapacity.

[
306
]

It is important to stress that the Court is not
called upon to evaluate whether the mother’s decision to disinherit Teresa was
right or appropriate. The contents of the wills are pleaded as evidence that
she was unduly influenced and as evidence that she lacked capacity:

[24]
La
raisonnabilité ou la déraisonnabilité des dispositions testamentaires
attaquées, par rapport au contexte de vie et des relations du testateur avec sa
famille ou son entourage sont des facteurs que le Tribunal aura à apprécier,
avec d'autres, pour décider s'il y a eu captation
.
[147]

[
307
]

The Court will review the contents of the wills
and codicils and the context in which the wills and codicils were executed to
assess whether it can conclude that the mother must have been unduly influenced
or must have lacked capacity.

i.          will dated March 16, 2009

[
308
]

The first contested will is the will dated March
16, 2009.

[
309
]

It simply divides the estate equally amongst the
six children. It has the effect of cancelling the January 2008 codicil and
going back to the August 2005 will.

[
310
]

The history of those wills is also relevant.
Prior to 2005, the parents’ wills divided the estate unevenly. In August 2005,
the parents executed wills that divided the estate evenly. The Court finds as a
matter of fact that the execution of the will in August 2005 led to the break
with Teresa. Her version, that the break occurred earlier in the summer when
the parents refused to execute mandates, and that the wills and mandates were
executed after the break, is not convincing.

[
311
]

Moreover, the Court dismisses Teresa’s argument
that the equal division of the estate is unfair because it fails to recognize
that she gave up her career to look after her parents. The evidence of Teresa’s
career was limited at best, and she appears to have received other benefits
from the arrangement such as living rent-free in the upper duplex. In any
event, the parents had the right to divide their estates however they wanted.

[
312
]

The Court has concerns about the January 2008
codicils, which favoured Teresa and, to a lesser extent, Donna. Teresa brought
the parents to the notary’s office without telling any of the siblings, the
meeting at the notary’s was long, loud and contentious, and the codicils were
kept secret after they were signed.

[
313
]

As a result, the mother executing a new will to
cancel the January 2008 codicil and go back to the earlier August 2005 will is
not evidence of incapacity or of undue influence.

[
314
]

The fact that the will was executed so soon
after the father passed away is troublesome. However, the siblings only learned
of the existence of the January 2008 codicils when the father passed away, and
they testified that the mother wanted to execute a new will immediately. As a
result, that fact on its own is not sufficient to conclude that the will is
invalid.

ii.         will dated May 4, 2009

[
315
]

The second contested will is dated May 4, 2009.

[
316
]

The content is identical to the March 14, 2009
will: the estate is divided equally among the six children. For the same
reasons as stated above, that division of the estate is not evidence of
incapacity or of undue influence.

[
317
]

The trigger for the execution of this will is
the disclosure by the mother on April 30, 2009 that Teresa brought her to a
notary in April. The mother did not remember exactly what she had executed, but
wanted to fix it. The siblings brought her to Notary Durso and she executed a
new will and mandate identical to what she had executed on March 14, 2009.

[
318
]

In fact, the mother executed only a mandate
before Notary Salama, with the result that the May 4, 2009 will was
unnecessary.

[
319
]

Teresa pleads that the mother’s confusion as to
what she had executed on April 8, 2009 should raise a doubt as to her capacity
to execute a will.

[
320
]

The Court does not agree. The Court has no
evidence as to what happened in Notary Salama’s office and what, if anything,
was explained to the mother. The fact that Notary Salama did not testify raises
concerns.

[
321
]

As a result, the May 4, 2009 will is not
evidence of incapacity or of undue influence.

iii.        codicil
dated September 14, 2009

[
322
]

The codicil dated September 14, 2009 provides
that, in view of the problems caused by Teresa in relation to the father’s
estate, any legal fees and disbursements are to be deducted from Teresa’s share
of the mother’s estate and shared among the other five siblings.

[
323
]

The codicil was executed in the context of the
litigation relating to the father’s estate. The siblings testify that the
mother was very upset with Teresa’s failure to cooperate with respect to the
estate. She was very upset that the estate was incurring legal fees and,
according to the siblings, she decided that Teresa should pay those expenses.
These events were contemporaneous with the execution of the codicil.

[
324
]

There is nothing in the execution of the will in
these circumstances that leads to the conclusion that the codicil is invalid.

iv.        will dated March 26, 2010

[
325
]

In the final will, the mother disinherited
Teresa. The testator has the absolute right to leave his or her estate to whomever
he or she chooses. The fact that it seems harsh or unfair is not sufficient to
conclude it resulted from the exercise of undue influence.
[148]

[
326
]

There are a number of circumstances surrounding
the execution of this final will that could lead to the conclusion that the
mother was unduly influenced by the siblings:

•

The mother had some degree of cognitive
impairment;

•

The triggering event for this will appears to be
a conversation started by Jadwiga during Christmas lunch;

•

The letter dated December 28, 2009 was drafted
by Richard and the language used is excessive;

•

All of the events alleged against Teresa in the
letter occurred prior to the execution of the September 2009 codicil;

•

Notary Durso refused to prepare a new will; and

•

Richard and Jadwiga took a number of steps over
three months to get the will executed.

[
327
]

Teresa puts much weight on the letter dated
December 28, 2009. She argues that it is not what it appears to be: it seems to
be a letter written by the mother in English, but in fact it was dictated by the
mother to Richard in a mix of English and Polish and was then rewritten by
Richard in English and translated into Polish.
[149]

She adds that the sheer venom and excess in the letter is not what a normal
mother would write about her first-born daughter, who was the primary
care-giver for her and her husband in their old age.

[
328
]

However, these circumstances are not conclusive
of undue influence:

•

The conversation at Christmas 2009 can be seen
as an innocent conversation about a friend of the mother’s;

•

Even if the conversation was intended to suggest
to the mother that she disinherit Teresa, it does not rise to the standard of
undue influence;

•

MacDonald testified that he was present when the
letter was drafted and he signed as a witness on both the English and the
Polish versions of the letter, even though he does not speak any Polish, and
that the mother was in agreement with it;

•

The events described in the letter do have some
element of truth and explain why the mother might have been sufficiently angry
with Teresa to disinherit her. In other words, the mother’s attitude towards
Teresa may have been unfair or harsh, but it “was not without a rational
foundation”;
[150]

•

Notary Durso was approaching retirement and
might not have wanted to get involved in a potentially litigious matter;

•

Notary Swierzbinska met the mother with Richard
and alone. She asked the mother about her wishes and she testified that the
mother answered her questions without looking to Richard, and that she gave the
same answers when Richard was out of the room;

•

The siblings all deny any attempt to unduly
influence the mother, and no third party testified as to witnessing any attempt
by the siblings to influence the mother against Teresa.

[
329
]

The Defendants argued that the circumstances of
this case are similar to those in
Blain (Succession de)
, where the
testator disinherited one of his daughters following an argument with her. The
evidence established that another daughter brought him to the notary and may
have encouraged him to disinherit her sister. The Court dismissed the action
seeking the nullity of the codicil and stated:

[58]

Bref, rien dans la preuve présentée au Tribunal ne s’apparente, de
près ou de loin, à de la captation ou de la manipulation de la part de Marquise
afin d’obtenir un avantage.

[59]

Au contraire, l’élément déclencheur de la signature du Codicille fut
plutôt l’altercation entre Diane et son conjoint, d’une part, et Théodore,
d’autre part, survenue quelques semaines avant la signature du Codicille, alors
que Théodore fut traité de «vieux christ [sic]
d’hypocrite».

[60]

Théodore fut insulté et a réagi fermement en excluant Diane du
Testament, comme il l’avait fait d’ailleurs, en 1988, après le décès de sa
première conjointe, la mère de ses quatre filles, vu l’attitude négative de
Diane face à sa mère.

[61]

Qui plus est, il est apparu clairement au Tribunal que Théodore
était lucide lorsqu’il a signé le Codicille devant Me Desmarais. Il voulait
tout simplement exclure du Testament, une fois pour toute, Diane, qui
l’indisposait, ainsi que son entourage immédiat.

[62]

À savoir s’il était justifié d’être ainsi indisposé lui appartenait
entièrement, et il ne revient pas au Tribunal de remettre en question le
jugement de Théodore à cet égard.
[151]

[
330
]

In light of all of the evidence, the Court
recognizes that it is
possible
that the siblings unduly influenced the
mother. They had the opportunity to do so, the mother had some degree of
cognitive impairment, the terms of the final will are harsh, and the siblings
benefitted from the new will.

[
331
]

However, the Court is not satisfied on the
balance of probabilities that it is
likely
that the siblings unduly
influenced the mother. The burden of proving undue influence is on Teresa, and
she has failed to meet that burden.

Conclusions

[
332
]

As a result of all of the foregoing, the Court
will dismiss Teresa’s action to cancel the wills.

[
333
]

Since Teresa is not a beneficiary under the
final will, she has no interest to ask for an inventory of the estate and an
accounting of the administration of the estate, or to ask for the replacement
of Richard and Jadwiga as liquidators of the mother’s estate. In any event,
there is no evidence to suggest that they are not fulfilling their duties as
liquidators.

[
334
]

Further, there is no basis for punitive damages
or for a condemnation for costs.

[
335
]

However, given the nature of the dispute, the
Court will exercise its discretion and dismiss the action without costs.

FINAL
NOTE

[
336
]

In his closing argument, Teresa’s lawyer
characterized this case as a family tragedy. The Court agrees. It is
unfortunate that the mother chose to disinherit Teresa. It is equally if not
more unfortunate that the parties failed to resolve the question among
themselves.

FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT:

[
337
]

DISMISSES
the
action;

338
]
